result:
There is a certain type of quiet that only exists at 35,000 feet. 

I am thinking about this right now, looking out of an airplane window at an endless, bruised-purple twilight. Down there, beneath the blanket of clouds, the world is spinning in its usual chaotic rhythm. There are traffic jams, coffees being spilled, arguments being had, emails being typed, and breaths being taken. But from up here, the world looks like a perfectly still, dimly lit map.

It’s profound, the way distance flattens complexity. From this altitude, you can't see the borders that humanity has violently drawn and defended for centuries. There are no countries, no toll booths, no gated communities—just the slow, geographical crawl of mountains and the shimmering, restless skin of the ocean. 

We are so obsessed with our own loudness. We fill our lives with glowing screens and notifications, terrified of the void, terrified of being left alone with our own heartbeats. But the Earth itself operates in a profound, patient silence. The tectonic plates shift beneath us with a stealth that takes millennia. The rain falls, eroding mountains grain by grain, not caring who owns the deed to the land. We are just borrowing space on a rock that is hurling through the cold dark of space, and we spend our brief, bright lifetimes arguing over the rental agreement.

From up here, the complexities of life shrink. The things I worried about in the terminal—the slightly passive-aggressive tone of a text message, the looming deadlines, the existential dread of turning another year older—feel wonderfully, mercifully small. Not insignificant, perhaps, but part of a larger, quieter picture. 

We are all just passengers. Not just on this aluminum tube hurtling through the sky, but on the planet itself. 

The sun is finally setting completely, turning the horizon into a sharp, glowing line of molten orange against the deep indigo of the stratosphere. Soon, the cabin lights will dim, and the people around me will fall asleep, illuminated only by the occasional flashing of a passing beacon on the wing. 

For now, I think I will just press my forehead against the cold acrylic of the window. I will breathe, and I will watch the dark world turn.
